extracted.intended_audience: writers, writing-students, and participants in creative-writing workshops or peer critique groups
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for giving and receiving peer critiques of creative writing in workshops or feedback groups, covering reading strategies, question prompts, sensitivity to writer needs, and how to frame suggestions. Meant for workshop participants and writing students.

rubrics_metrics.name: First read — read as a pure consumer
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the piece through the first time as a pure consumer, for interest and hopefully enjoyment. Try to give yourself over to the piece. See what is there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After finishing the piece note how you feel about it. What is your overall feeling or impression? What are the first things that come to your mind about the piece? Write these first general impressions at the end of the piece for the writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second read — consciously read more critically
rubrics_metrics.description: Now consciously read the piece through more critically. This second effort really requires critical thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Critical’ does not mean negative; it means applying a different way of thinking based in your feelings and responses to identify things that didn’t work and to try to figure out why. Some people combine the two stages quickly, but beware of stopping at the first (consumer) stage and not doing the harder work of critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust approach to the piece's development and needs
rubrics_metrics.description: One piece may be whole and nearly perfect whereas another may be just struggling into existence. We cannot approach these two manuscripts in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the piece needs a macro approach (themes, overall structure) or a micro approach (language, first paragraph, establishing voice), or a combination. Also consider the writer’s emotional need—some need affirmation to proceed, others want heavy criticism—and be sensitive and adjustable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the terms of the piece (writer's intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: One thing I always ask myself in responding to a piece of writing is: What are the terms of this piece? In other words, what is the writer trying to do?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It’s nearly impossible to have a helpful response if you don’t understand the terms. Identify whether the piece aims to be analytical, humorous, lyrical, etc., and critique in light of those intentions rather than imposing unrelated standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate success relative to the piece's own terms
rubrics_metrics.description: So the questions become, What are the terms of this piece? Does the writer meet them?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t simply ask 'why not' or reject the terms wholesale; if a technique isn’t working (example: abstract, distanced first-person that fails to engage), suggest alternatives that respect the writer’s aims (for example, trying third person) rather than only saying 'It didn’t work for me.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement: Did this engage me? Why or why not?
rubrics_metrics.description: Did this engage me? Why or why not?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect on your emotional/attentive response and articulate specific reasons for engagement or lack thereof so the writer knows what connects and what doesn't.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention/Interest throughout: Did it hold my attention?
rubrics_metrics.description: Did this hold my attention throughout? Where was I most engaged and why?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify parts of the piece that sustained interest and analyze what made them effective (scene, detail, voice, momentum) so the writer can amplify those strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and information gaps: Are things confusing or missing?
rubrics_metrics.description: Are any things confusing to me? Could I follow the piece, or were there gaps, or need for more information? What else did I need to know?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out places where readers get lost or where additional detail/context would help understanding or emotional payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening effectiveness: How effective is first sentence/paragraph?
rubrics_metrics.description: What about the opening? Did the piece draw me in? How effective is the first sentence and first paragraph and why or why not? Did I want to keep reading?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the opening establishes voice, stakes, tone, or curiosity appropriate to the piece’s terms, and suggest concrete ways to strengthen it if it fails to hook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace and movement: Do things move along and at the right pace?
rubrics_metrics.description: Do things move along? What is the pace of the piece, and why?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess pacing decisions against the piece's aims (e.g., deliberate slowness for mood vs. too slow because of exposition). Refer back to the terms of the piece when judging pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and voice: How would you describe the language?
rubrics_metrics.description: What about language? How would you describe it? How does it function in terms of what you feel the writer is trying to do?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment on diction, sentence rhythm, tone, figurative language, and whether voice serves or undermines the piece’s intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is coming across: themes, meaning, emotional impact
rubrics_metrics.description: What are you 'getting' from the piece? This could be any number of things, but it’s really helpful for you to feed back to the writer what is coming across for you—story or meaning or themes or emotional impact or enjoyment or whatever-wise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell the writer what landed for you so they know how readers are interpreting their work and where intended effects are succeeding or failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the critic: be a reader not the author
rubrics_metrics.description: You’re not being asked to be the final word on a piece or to write it for the writer. You’re only being asked to be what you already are, a good reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid prescribing exactly how the writer must fix things; offer observations, reactions, and possible approaches without taking over the author's choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give feedback sensitively and avoid overwhelming the writer
rubrics_metrics.description: We have to be sensitive and adjustable regarding every piece of writing. There is also our sense of the writer, whether she wants and need a lot of criticism or needs basically affirmation in order to proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the amount and tone of critique to the writer’s state and the piece’s condition—some pieces/writers need encouragement; others need tough notes. Balance honesty with tact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiving criticism: listen first and keep an open mind
rubrics_metrics.description: When receiving criticism, do better if you simply listen, at first, before you 'pollute' the conversation about my piece with my explanations, apologies, defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After initial responses, enter the dialogue. Keep an open mind and do not react too strongly; recognize that suggestions are oblique and indirect and not meant to be taken too literally at first. Value of criticism may take time to sink in (David Huddle: 'stories yearn towards a state of perfection... it is up to a critic to help the author discern the story’s desires').
